commit message:
fix(setup): resolve macos code-signing errors when installing pip packages

On my Mac (M4 Pro, macOS 26.3 Tahoe), BlenderProc failed on first run
with "Operation not permitted" errors. Two issues:

1. custom-python-packages is created inside the Blender.app bundle,
   which macOS seals via code-signing. Any attempt to mkdir or write
   files inside the .app fails with PermissionError.

2. The pip upgrade (pip install --upgrade pip) destroys pip entirely.
   What happens: pip first uninstalls itself (e.g. 23.2.1) from
   Blender's site-packages — deletion succeeds. Then it tries to
   install the new version into the same sealed location — which
   fails. The rollback also fails because the directory is still
   read-only. Result: no working pip at all, and every subsequent
   package install breaks with "No module named pip".

Fix (1): when the default packages path doesn't already exist and its
parent directory isn't writable, walk up the path to find the .app
boundary and place custom-python-packages as a sibling directory
outside the bundle. If the directory already exists (e.g. user
previously granted Full Disk Access), the original path is preserved
for backward compatibility.

Fix (2): after attempting the pip upgrade, verify pip still works. If
it was destroyed by a failed upgrade, re-run ensurepip to restore the
bundled version. This is a no-op on systems where the upgrade succeeds.

fixes #768

commit message:
Get env:USER in a more reliable way

In some environment like Docker, $USER might not be set
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/54411218/docker-why-isnt-user-environment-variable-set
`getpass.getuser` checks the environment variables LOGNAME, USER, LNAME and USERNAME, in order, and returns the value of the first one which is set to a non-empty string. If none are set, the login name from the password database is returned on systems which support the pwd module, otherwise, an exception is raised.

commit message:
fix(types): Do not apply `scale` twice on primitive

Up to now, `scale` is applied in `create_primitive()` to the
primitive after its creation. The reason for this was a bug in
Blender which ignored the `scale` argument in
`bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_..._add()`. This seems to be fixed by now,
so the scaling inside BlenderProc results in applying the scaling
twice.

This commit fixes this bug in BlenderProc by deleting the second
scaling.

commit message:
feat(blender): make depth, distance and segmentation output rgb in blender 4.1

Since Blender 4.1 the .exr depth outputs are one channel
instead of three channels. The imageio.v3.imread
using 'opencv' can't open single channel .exr. Thus
using nodes we create three channel image output
from the depth again.

This might be fixed in future versions of Blender, fix
to respect the file foramt 'Color' property (that's actually set to RGB)
was already merged into master:

https://projects.blender.org/blender/blender/commit/40be124184bb571669b7346a36003c33c412cb20

commit message:
fix(blenderproc): Fix __init__.py for Windows

Currently, the stack summary is check on startup of BlenderProc,
in order to determine whether it has been called correctly (i.e.
either via the `blenderproc` command or the command line script.
This has not worked on Windows, since the stack trace differs
from the one on Linux, and hence an exception is thrown by
__init__.py.

This commit fixes this issue by performing different checks of
the stack trace depending on the current OS. Additionally, the
check for Linux was rewritten to be understandable more easily.

Fixes #358

These planets have been validated using a statistical method. The
planet's parameters are not well constrained. However the FPP is below 1
percent, which is why I think we can call them confirmed.

Most of the files have been created using a script from a csv table
provided by the Kepler Team. Some systems, those with previously known
planets have been edited manually.

Note that the Kepler team has introduced some confusion regarding the
planet names. For example, a three planet system may now have planets
named like this:
KOI-123 b
KOI-123 c
Kepler-45 b
We'll have to see how that works out.

New planets have currently a new-tag. I'll remove that later. It's just
for now to keep track of what's going on.

commit message:
Gliese 436: the planet candidate UCF-1.01 is not considered confirmed in the
discovery paper.

The designation "Gliese 436 c" was previously used for hypothetical outer
planet candidates invoked to explain various properties about the planet
Gliese 436 b (e.g. maintenance of orbital eccentricity, claimed transit
variations). The discovery paper notes that UCF-1.01 would be called
Gliese 436 c if confirmed, but so far this has not happened. The assignment of
the designation Gliese 436 c to this candidate is therefore not supported.

Stevenson et al. (2012): http://cdsads.u-strasbg.fr/abs/2012ApJ...755....9S

commit message:
Added hint for python version

The script only runs under python 2.x.
python 3.x:
# python 3.x
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET, urllib.request, gzip, io
url = "https://github.com/OpenExoplanetCatalogue/oec_gzip/raw/master/systems.xml.gz"
oec = ET.parse(gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=io.BytesIO(urllib.request.urlopen(url).read())))

# Output mass and radius of all planets 
for planet in oec.findall(".//planet"):
    print(planet.findtext("mass"), planet.findtext("radius"))

# Find all circumbinary planets 
for planet in oec.findall(".//binary/planet"):
    print(planet.findtext("name"))

# Output distance to planetary system (in pc, if known) and number of planets in system
for system in oec.findall(".//system"):
    print(system.findtext("distance"), len(system.findall(".//planet")))

author: David Laehnemann <david.laehnemann@hhu.de>
commit message:
fix: add more logging statemens to `sleuth-diffexp.R`, add QuantSeq testing data to get QuantSeq tests to pass (#86)

The underlying problem that we identified with the work on this
`debug-vroom` branch was a malformatted `custom` file for specifying
canonical transcript to use in `sleuth-diffexp.R`. The take-away message
here were:

1. The `sleuth-diffexp.R` script with its large `write_results()`
function was hard to debug, and to ease the burden a bit in the future,
we should probably keep the extra logging statements we included.
2. The `datavzrd/diffexp-template.yaml` does not seem to play nice with
`custom` canonical transcript files. The `canonical` column does not
make sense in the `genes_aggregated` results table (as this should only
contain gene names / identifiers, and no transcript identifiers, and
only the latter could be canonical or not), so we remove it there.
However, how to have a `canonical` column in the `genes_representative`
case with a `custom` canonical transcript file still needs to be solved
before merging this PR.

```
  File "~/mambaforge/envs/snakemake/lib/python3.10/site-packages/snakemake/__init__.py", line 22, in <module>
    from snakemake.target_jobs import parse_target_jobs_cli_args
  File "~/mambaforge/envs/snakemake/lib/python3.10/site-packages/snakemake/target_jobs.py", line 4, in <module>
    from snakemake.common import parse_key_value_arg
  File "~/mambaforge/envs/snakemake/lib/python3.10/site-packages/snakemake/common/__init__.py", line 284, in <module>
    @contextlib.asynccontextmanager
AttributeError: module 'contextlib' has no attribute 'asynccontextmanager'
```

Tried running under Python 3.10 and 3.7, still encountered the same
issue, but eventually tracked the rabbit hole down to this.

Updating the wrapper for cutadapt slightly changes the syntax, but no
modification to the config.yaml file is needed. Additionally,
(optionally) I added multithreading, as cutadapt scales quite well.

commit message:
fix: canonical transcript mapped read extraction (#77)

The main aim of this PR is to get the extraction of reads mapped to the
canonical transcripts in the `rule get_mapped_canonical_transcripts`
down from about 44GB of memory usage regardless of the input BAM file
size and hours of grepping, down to seconds / minutes of extraction time
with almost no memory footprint. This happens here:

https://github.com/snakemake-workflows/rna-seq-kallisto-sleuth/compare/fix-canonical-transcript-mapped-read-extraction?expand=1#diff-6562a38fb77f8839a8731b8a882bf0d0b683d6268cdffb433dcbe1f360ccedc4R103

This required using a BED file, and thus I switched to generating a
valid BED file in the `rule get_canonical_ids` and switched to using
that BED file for keeping track of transcript strand information instead
of hacking this into the contig names of the reference fasta file. This
lead to some cleanup in the workflow.

Other things that happened along the way are:
* removed an unnecessary `r-dplyr` dependency, as this is pulled in by
`r-tidyverse` anyways
* cleaned up file names to more clearly reflect what they contain
* cleaned up variable / column names in python script to use only
lowercase letters
* removed some redundancy in wrapper calling by re-`use`ing the
`samtools index` rule -- thus, we only have to update the wrapper
version in one place and all instances should always stay in sync

For now, this is not yet tested. So I'll mark this as a draft to start
with. But I wanted it up here to be able to test it on different setups
by checking out the branch.

commit message:
fix: move summing of go-term fold changes out of log-space (#141)

As [discussed in a separate pull
request](https://github.com/snakemake-workflows/rna-seq-kallisto-sleuth/pull/136#discussion_r1983484603),
it seems like we are currently multiplying fold changes across the genes
within a GO term, as we are adding up `log2()` transformations of the
fold changes. To get a sum instead of a product, we have to first take
`2^<log2()-value>`. And if we want to end up with a log2-value of the
sum, we afterwards have to take the `log2()` again. This is what this
pull request suggests.

Not sure though, if this is exactly what we want. Two things we might do
differently are:
1. We might want to leave the fold change in non-log space. But thinking
about this again, we need log2 fold changes for the (signed) pi value
calculation, right?
2. We might want to normalize for the number of genes in a GO term.
Otherwise, a ranking of GO terms based on the signed pi value will
easily be dominated by high level GO terms that simply encompass a lot
of genes. I'll put in a review comment with the respective suggestion.

commit message:
fix: add support for drosophila melanogaster and other non-standard species (#142)

I noticed two errors that occured while working with RNA-Seq data from
Drosophila melanogaster and tried to fix them:


[1](https://github.com/snakemake-workflows/rna-seq-kallisto-sleuth/commit/698a4790b51cb25827cfc4c7769efe08b13ace19).
Gene names for the fruit fly can sometimes have a colon in them, when
belonging to a gene family (e.g. His4:CG33869 and His4:CG31611). This
leads to an error when selecting the correct name and value in
postprocess_go_enrichment.py as they are also separated by a colon. The
separation then results in three parts (His4, CG33869, 0.73842) instead
of two parts.

[2](https://github.com/snakemake-workflows/rna-seq-kallisto-sleuth/commit/075315f266a2e117a3a5dd0f8f1b4c338ac7a450).
For Drosophila melanogaster the "ensembl_transcript_id_version"
attribute from the Ensembl mart does not exist. This attribute is part
of the 3-prime attributes which (I assume?) are not needed for standard
RNA-Seq analysis.

Use PLT when calling sigsetjmp on i386

With gcc-10, the linkes issues a warning when trying to call sigsetjmp
directly on i386:

libos.a(zsvjmp.o): warning: relocation against `__sigsetjmp@@GLIBC_2.0' in read-only section `.text'
/usr/bin/ld: warning: creating DT_TEXTREL in a PIE

This can be avoided to use the Procedure Linkage Table for this
function. Note that other architectures still use direct calls:

 * ARM 32/64 bit
 * MIPS 32/64 bit
 * PowerPC 64 bit

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Fix allocated size of Dimblock

Generally, the size of a structure is not just the sum of the sizes of
its members, since padding may require additional space. For
`Dimblock`, this is the case, since the first member is an `int`, and
the next one is a pointer: on 64-bit platforms, `int` is 4 bytes,
while pointers are 8 bytes and therefore 4 bytes padding are inserted.

This patch fixes the allocated size by using the real size of the
structure.

Also, the length of the `dims` member is set to unspecified, to avoid
compilers to optimize out the access to the member.

author: Patrick Wallace - STFC UKRI <patrick.wallace@STFC.AC.UK>
commit message:
SLALIB bug

To whom it may concern...

I have discovered a decades-old bug in the SLALIB routine sla_EQEQX:

https://github.com/Starlink/starlink/blob/master/libraries/sla/eqeqx.f

It causes observed places (the direction of the incoming radiation
from a celestial source) to be wrong by an amount that was zero at
J2000.0 but grows steadily and at the present time has reached
almost 0.1 arcseconds.

Corrected code (including the test program) is attached.  For
anyone interested, the story is as follows.

* Using the classical pre IAU 2000 equinox based methods, hour
  angles are obtained by subtracting apparent right ascension from
  the local apparent sidereal time.

* The local apparent sidereal time involves the quantity "equation
  of the equinoxes", which is the difference between mean and
  apparent sidereal time.

* Most of the equation of the equinoxes comes from the nutation in
  longitude.

* The previous, incorrect, sla_EQEQX obtained the nutation
  components by calling the routine sla_NUTC.

* sla_NUTC implements the nutation model of Shirai & Fukushima
  (2001).

* Shirai & Fukushima included in their nutation model a secular
  term that compensated for the imperfect precession model in use
  at that time.  Thus the combination of IAU 1976 precession and
  the Shirai & Fukushima delivered milliarcsecond accuracy apparent
  places, which is good.

* However, this secular term has no place in the computation of the
  nutation per se, and has been polluting SLALIB's computation of
  sidereal time.

* The cure is simply to fall back on the nutation model that
  predates Shirai & Fukushima (2001), namely the IAU 1980 model.

* The fix to sla_EQEQX has been simply to call sla_NUTC80 instead
  of sla_NUTC.

* The corrected sla_EQEQX delivers equation of the equinoxes values
  that agree to better than 1 mas with more recent algorithms.

I doubt there are any applications out there where this bug has had
any practical effect.  The pollution has been smooth and gradual,
and is at least an order of magnitude below the level important for
telescope pointing;  in any case, pointing models have probably been
fudging it out.  The most critical would probably be interferometer
delays, and such applications really ought to be using modern post
IAU 2000 CIO based algorithms.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Add a trailing `\n` to the end of variable format strings.

f2c does not recognize the length of a variable FORMAT string and will
try to read the string until a non-blank appears.

The format strings are declared as `CHARACTER*8` and do not
automatically have a `\0` appended at the end. Therefore, when the
string is filled with blanks until the end, it will read one char over
the end (which is hopefully a non-blank).

This is probably a bug in f2c; however it is not fixed in the recent
versions as well. To work around this, a trailing `\0` is
automatically added.

commit message:
Replace vfork() with fork()

vfork() is marked obsolete in POSIX.1-2001 and was removed from Posix
in POSIX.1-2008. Newer macOS compilers warn about this, so we remove
it. vfork was used in Debian only for speed improvements by avoiding
copying the address space; however modern systems use copy-on-write,
this argument is not actual anymore.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Replace readline library by libedit on MacOS X

Libedit is available as a standard package on MacOSX:

https://opensource.apple.com/source/libedit/

as well as on all Linux distributions. Its license is BSD-3-Clause.
Another option is the "editline" library which is available on Linux
(seems to be outdated, but may be a good replacement for static
linking due to its size).

All three are compatible and can be replaced by changing library in
the linking step of ecl:

 * readline "-lreadline"
 * libedit  "-ledit"
 * editline "-leditline"

References:

* readline https://tiswww.cwru.edu/php/chet/readline/rltop.html
* libedit  http://thrysoee.dk/editline/
* editline https://github.com/troglobit/editline

Since readline is standard on Linux, and there is also a compatibility package
for readline5, we use editline only on MacOS X; however we use the system
provided readline on Linux and therefore can remove its sources from IRAF.

We also clean up the mkpkg file a bit and remove SPARC and STScI specific
stuff.

author: Mike Fitzpatrick <mjfitzpatrick@gmail.com>
commit message:
revert to CFITSIO for table i/o

The libtbtables.a was changed in v2.16 to use SPP fitsio from earlier uses
of the fortran version under the assumption that they were equivalent.
However, there is a bug in the fortran version of ftdrow() when called
by the TDIFFER task in which the output table doesn't have its NAXIS2
value properly updated for FITS tables causing the task to exit.  The
cfitsio code acknowledges the value may not be correct and so uses an
internal data structure value for the 'nrows' rather than the keyword,
but equivalent functionality does not exist in the fortran version.  A
similar problem exists when inserting rows but this is not called from
any existing NTTOOLS tasks.

This change fixes a bug in the GEMINI.GSEEING task which is the only
task known to call TDIFFER.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Fix linenum calculation in xpp

First, when `begin` is parsed, the end of line `\n` is not eaten
up. In fact, there may be code following after `begin` on the same
line; this is placed after xpp in the line after `begin`. If nothing
follows the `begin` statement on the same line, an empty line is
added. This means, that `linenum` must __not__ increased here; it is
increased when the `\n` of this line is found.

Similar argument for parsing a `task` line; `linenum` must
__not__increased here as well.

When parsing `.help` ... `.endhelp` however, one `linenum` increase was
missing, which is added now.

Definitvely use flex to generate unix/generix/lexyy.c

versions. While f.e. on Debian Buster, it creates

the version found on SuseLeap 15.1 generates

Using `extern char *yytext` in `generic.c` then creates a segfault.
To ensure that we use the right dialect, we explicitly use "flex".

commit message:
- Added an `inconsistency-check' mechanism to f77.sh, setup.sh and Makefile.
 + `make check_iraf' performs the `inconsistency-check' of SPP or FORTRAN 
   sources between a function definition and callers.  The GCC output may 
   output messages like this:
    * "warning: passing arg x of `xxx_' from incompatible pointer type"
    * "error: too few arguments to function `xxx_'"
    * "error: too many arguments to function `xxx_'"
   These messages help improve SPP and FORTRAN codes for LP64-SPP.
- Appended complete macros for the `inconsistency-check' to knames.h.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Use "macos64" for non-intel 64 bit macOS architectures

For Intel, we still keep the old name "macintel" for backward
compatibility; but for ARM64 (and possibly for other 64-bit macOS
architectures) we use a common name.

This is similar to the philosophy in Linux and FreeBSD: Encode only OS
name and 32/64 bit, but not the CPU architecture.

On this occasion, also remove some architectures which are really outdated

better portability.

The only place where SIGFUNC is still there is one place zxwhen.c,
because here the call signature is different.

commit message:
photcal: Fix access to fit parameter table

The parameter table contains all fit parameters. These are changed by
the fit subroutine (NLFIT), which expects to have them in a
homogenious "real" (4 byte) array, with subsequent entries directly
neighored. Therefore, the array cannot be set with `Memr[P2R(base+index)]`,
but needs to be set with `Memr[P2R(base)+index]`. This patch changes
this in a consistent way.

commit message:
Removed "mem_=0" setting and appends a trick to f77.sh.
This trick enables valid memory access without "mem_=0".

These modification are required to solve errors reported by
new GNU linker on x86_64 Linux.

(example of error)
/XXX/src/iraf/lib/libstg.a(t_gkideco.o): In function `tgkide_':
t_gkideco.c:(.text+0xdc): relocation truncated to fit: R_X86_64_32
against symbol `mem_' defined in *ABS* section
in /tmp/T_x_stdgraph.e.rDqM6m

Therefore, other FORTRAN compilers (gfortran, g77, etc.) can no
longer be used for IRAF, since "mem_=0" cannot be used.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Simplify ZGMTCO

The original code is broken due to a number of assumptions taken in
the code:

 * It assumes Jan 1 1980 as being without daylight saving time, which
   is not generally true on the southern hemisphere.
 * It assumes that the offset did not change (except for DST) since
   1980, which is not generally true: F.e. the time zone "Europe/Kiev"
   changed the offset from UTC + 2 hours to UTC + 1 hour after the
   seggregation of the Soviet Union.
 * It assumes that daylight saving time is always 1 hour.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Add a trailing `\n` to the end of variable format strings.

f2c does not recognize the length of a variable FORMAT string and will
try to read the string until a non-blank appears.

The format strings are declared as `CHARACTER*8` and do not
automatically have a `\0` appended at the end. Therefore, when the
string is filled with blanks until the end, it will read one char over
the end (which is hopefully a non-blank).

This is probably a bug in f2c; however it is not fixed in the recent
versions as well. To work around this, a trailing `\0` is
automatically added.

It appears that the pointer was set to NULL anyway already for some unknown

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Handle negative pointer in garbage collector

Previously, the garbage collection in `mgc.x` used two pseudo values for
organizational issues: implicitly initialized NULL for the end of the `MGC`
buffer, and negative values for pointers that are already freed.

Since pointers may be negative (they are relative to the `Mem` common block),
this patch changes this behaviour: we now use NULL for pointers that are
already freed, and an additional variable `bmax` in the `/nmemio/` common
block to determine current the end of the `MGC` buffer.

Note that this could not be fully tested, since the garbage collector
is active only when the environment variable `MEMIO_COLLECT` is set to
1. This mode is however already buggy with the precompiled version
2.16.1:

```
$ MEMIO_COLLECT=1 cl
setting terminal type to 'xgterm' ...

PANIC in `/iraf/iraf/bin/64/bin.linux64/x_system.e': invalid SET in IRAF Main
```

commit message:
revert to CFITSIO for table i/o

The libtbtables.a was changed in v2.16 to use SPP fitsio from earlier uses
of the fortran version under the assumption that they were equivalent.
However, there is a bug in the fortran version of ftdrow() when called
by the TDIFFER task in which the output table doesn't have its NAXIS2
value properly updated for FITS tables causing the task to exit.  The
cfitsio code acknowledges the value may not be correct and so uses an
internal data structure value for the 'nrows' rather than the keyword,
but equivalent functionality does not exist in the fortran version.  A
similar problem exists when inserting rows but this is not called from
any existing NTTOOLS tasks.

This change fixes a bug in the GEMINI.GSEEING task which is the only
task known to call TDIFFER.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Replace "OpenDetachedProcess" with "ForkDetachedProcess" in CL

For background operation, CL needs to start an identical copy of
itself. This was (unnecessarily) emulated by starting a new CL process
and restoring its internal state later.

On POSIX systems, this is not necessary, since the fork() system call
already provides an identical copy of the process.

To utilize the IRAF job management, the fork call needs to be wrapped
in several levels:

- unix/os/zopdr.c provides a SPP callable C interface of fork()
- sys/etc/prfodpr.x is the SPP implementation (incl. job management)
- sys/libc/cprdet.c provides a C interface to the SPP function
- pkg/*cl/bkg.c finally calls that

And one has to provide the naming transition as well.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Avoid using ECHO in generic's token parser

ECHO does an unconditional output. When processing a condition with f.e.

    $for (rd)
    $if (datatype == r)
        if (IS_INDEFD(GM_XO(fit)))
           call gsset (sf1, GSXREF, INDEFR)
    $endif
    $endfor

then we want the output for IS_INDEFD and INDEFR only while processing
"r" (real). When INDEF(R|D|...) is causing an ECHO, this results in
additional "INDEFDINDEFR" in the output.

Replacing ECHO with outstr(yytext) solves the problem.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Add fork() infrastructure to the IRAF system libs

For background operation, CL needs to start an identical copy of
itself. This was (unnecessarily) emulated by starting a new CL process
and restoring its internal state later.

On POSIX systems, this is not necessary, since the fork() system call
already provides an identical copy of the process.

To utilize the IRAF job management, the fork call needs to be wrapped
in several levels:

- unix/os/zopdr.c provides ZFODPR(), a SPP callable C interface of fork()
- sys/etc/prfodpr.x has PRFODPR, the SPP implementation (incl. job management)
- sys/libc/cprdet.c provides c_prfodpr(), a C interface to the SPP function
- pkg/*cl/bkg.c will finally call that.

And one has to provide the naming transition as well.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Handle negative pointer in garbage collector

Previously, the garbage collection in `mgc.x` used two pseudo values for
organizational issues: implicitly initialized NULL for the end of the `MGC`
buffer, and negative values for pointers that are already freed.

Since pointers may be negative (they are relative to the `Mem` common block),
this patch changes this behaviour: we now use NULL for pointers that are
already freed, and an additional variable `bmax` in the `/nmemio/` common
block to determine current the end of the `MGC` buffer.

Note that this could not be fully tested, since the garbage collector
is active only when the environment variable `MEMIO_COLLECT` is set to
1. This mode is however already buggy with the precompiled version
2.16.1:

```
$ MEMIO_COLLECT=1 cl
setting terminal type to 'xgterm' ...

PANIC in `/iraf/iraf/bin/64/bin.linux64/x_system.e': invalid SET in IRAF Main
```

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Fix type of arguments for IRAF_MAIN

IRAF_MAIN is an SPP (and therefore FORTRAN)
procedure (`sys/etc/main.x`). Some of its arguments are "int":

```
int procedure iraf_main (a_cmd, a_inchan, a_outchan, a_errchan,
	a_driver, a_devtype, prtype, bkgfile, jobcode, sys_runtask, onentry)

char	a_cmd[ARB]		# command to be executed or null string
int	a_inchan		# process standard input
int	a_outchan		# process standard output
int	a_errchan		# process standard error output
int	a_driver		# ZLOCPR address of device driver
int	a_devtype		# device type (text or binary)
int	prtype			# process type (connected, detached, host)
char	bkgfile[ARB]		# packed filename of bkg file if detached
int	jobcode			# jobcode if detached process
extern	sys_runtask()		# client task execution procedure
extern	onentry()		# client onentry procedure
```

This translates into "XINT *" as the required argument type in C (and
not "int *") when called in `sys/os/zmain.c`.

commit message:
Accept zero date in archives

A zero date is a valid (and not anymore unplausible) entry in an
library archive. Archives with that entries can f.e. created with
newer GNU ar and the `D` option, or when the
`--enable-deterministic-archives` option was set during the build of
ar.

To allow at least some updating, we use the last modified date of the library if the date is set to zero.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Fix pointer type for BYTMOV call

The last argument of BYTMOV is an `XINT *` (aka `long int *`, 64bit), while
`nbytes` is `int` (32 bit) only. Just (implicitly) changing pointer type
destroys the alignment and may raise an illegal access. On big endian, even
the wrong value is transferred.

Since the variable is not an output, we can just assing a temporary var with
the correct type.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Remove vtel subpackage from imred

vtel was used for the data reduction of the Kitt Peak Vacuum
Telescope.  After 29 years of solar imaging, the vacuum telescope was
decommissioned in 2002, which is 15 years ago.

The vtel subpackage uses a the "MRQMIN" routine which was copied from
the Numerical Recipes book. This code is not licensed for public
redistribution and must be removed from the public IRAF package. Since
the subpackage is specialized for data from an instrument that is out
of operation for a long time, it is not worth replacing the NR code
with free code.

Therefore, this patch removed the vtel package completely.

architecture (ISA) based on established reduced instruction set
computing (RISC) principles. While there are still no real hardware
CPUs available, there is already Linux support with it, and it exists
a Debian port.

This patch provides the assembler code in zsvjmp.S to support
riscv64. It is based on

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Fix linenum calculation in xpp

First, when `begin` is parsed, the end of line `\n` is not eaten
up. In fact, there may be code following after `begin` on the same
line; this is placed after xpp in the line after `begin`. If nothing
follows the `begin` statement on the same line, an empty line is
added. This means, that `linenum` must __not__ increased here; it is
increased when the `\n` of this line is found.

Similar argument for parsing a `task` line; `linenum` must
__not__increased here as well.

When parsing `.help` ... `.endhelp` however, one `linenum` increase was
missing, which is added now.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Fix type of variable to hold vo_paramNext() return value

`vo_paramNext()` returns an `int`, and specifically returns a negative value
if there are arguments left after processing the options.

Depending on the signedness of `char`, this may be converted to a positive
value if the return value is converted to a `char`. This happens f.e. on ARM
processors, where the char is `unsigned char` by default. Since the option
parsing is stopped when this is `<=0`, additional (non-option) arguments lead
to an errornous processing.

The correct type to hold the return value is `int`, and this was already set
in some VO applications (f.e. `votjoin`). This patch changes this for the
remaining apps.

This fixes the read problem of VOTables on arm processors.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Handle negative pointer in garbage collector

Previously, the garbage collection in `mgc.x` used two pseudo values for
organizational issues: implicitly initialized NULL for the end of the `MGC`
buffer, and negative values for pointers that are already freed.

Since pointers may be negative (they are relative to the `Mem` common block),
this patch changes this behaviour: we now use NULL for pointers that are
already freed, and an additional variable `bmax` in the `/nmemio/` common
block to determine current the end of the `MGC` buffer.

Fix declaration of cdsmem in rpp

This fixes a problem that rpp.e does not work correctly when build
with optimization: since cdsmem is initialized everywhere as `integer
mem(1)` the C compiler (after f2c) assumes that the variable is not an
array, but a pointer to a single variable, and any subsequent write
can be replaced by just writing the last value.

It should really be a `integer mem(60000)`.

author: Doug Tody <tody@noao.edu>
commit message:
Add an Alpha version of zsvjmp

The trick with this one, which I missed at first, was to set register
27 (pv) to the address of setjmp before branching into it. The alpha
procedure calling sequence assumes that the caller of a procedure does
this and it is required to set the global pointer correctly for the
procedure being executed.

The STScI version of zsvjmp (produced by technical support at DEC)
could not be used as it was just setjmp with the name changed.
The status argument used by zsvjmp was being ignored, and setjmp
was being called with the wrong jump buffer address.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Fix pointer type for ZCLSND call

The first argument of ZCLSND is an `XINT *` (aka `long int *`, 64bit), while
`vm_server` is `int` (32 bit) only. Just (implicitly) changing pointer type
destroys the alignment and may caise an illegal access of the address after
`*vmserver`. And on big endian, even the wrong value is transferred.

Since the variable is not an output, we can just assing a temporary var with
the correct type. And just adjust the type of the status var.

commit message:
Use the IRAF epoch as the base for zgmtco calculation

This reverts commit ef3151200c8422745a0d2c606e0260f05f036379.
and commit d23c020ccf4b2d2f47e3de376fb4407986d329e0.

and a few others. It basically reverts to the version 2.11.

zgmtco gives the time difference for the following numbers:

 * Seconds since 1980-01-01 local time ("LST")

 * Seconds since 1980-01-01 UTC ("GMT")

Both are (and should be) monotone, so the difference is just the
start. Therefore, we calculate the difference on the base of the begin
of the epoch.

Adding the current (!) summer time (as done in version 2.12) seems to
be a wrong idea here.

commit message:
Use O_RDONLY & Co. in open() calls

From the man page of open (2):

> ```
> int open(const char *pathname, int flags);
> ```
> [...]
>
> The argument flags must  include  one  of  the  following  access modes:
> `O_RDONLY`, `O_WRONLY`, or `O_RDWR`.  These request opening the file
> read-only, write-only, or read/write, respectively.

Some places in IRAF however use `0` for the flags when the file is
opened readonly. This fails in the moment when `O_RDONLY` is not `0`,
as on GNU HURD. Similar of `O_WRONLY` and `O_RDWR`.

This patch uses the pre-defined modes in these cases.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Fix buffer length in urlget.x

Sometimes, the HTTP response header is larger than SZ_PATHNAME (512
chars). This may happen especially when the URL redirects to a content
delivery service. In this case, the end of the redirected URL was
cut (resulting in a failing download), or the program even segfaulted.

This patch increases the size of the reply buffer to SZ_BUF (8192
chars), and also takes care that the program does not crash when the
header is larger. The response URL however is still limited to
SZ_LINE (1023 chars).

Note that these limits are still arbitrary and may be too short: the
maximum *recommended* size for an URL is 2048, and the http response
header has no size limit at all.  SZ_LINE is however builtin in many
places of string processing, so it is probably not easy to increase
the max URL size to the recommended one (except increasing SZ_LINE
itself).

commit message:
Fix cpu_time calculation in unix/os/zgtenv.c

This should return the CPU time in milliseconds. In early versions,
this was calculated as floating point cpu*1000./clkfreq with clkfreq
being the clock ticks per second. At some point, floating point was
tried to be avoided in the kernel, and so this got an (all integer)

    cpu * 1000 / clkfreq

To prevent (undiscovered) overflow for large values of cpu (namely
when cpu > MAX_LONG/1000), the order is reversed:

     cpu / clkfreq * 1000

Note that this is still the same operation, just a different order.

In version 2.15, determination of clkfreq seemed to be complicated,
and this got the buggy

    if (cpu > MAX_LONG/1000)
        *cpu_time = cpu / 10;
    else
        *cpu_time = cpu * 10;

which is wrong, because is assumes clkfreq=100, and it also does the
wrong thing for cpu > MAX_LONG/1000.

In POSIX, the clock frequency can be determined with
sysconf(_SC_CLK_TCK), which is used here now.

commit message:
Check that isascii() is true before doing any other isXXXXX() test

The IRAF libc maintaines the array of character types as a `char[128]`. So,
any test that uses this array should ensure that the argument is in this
range. This is now done by preceding all tests with `isascii(c) &&`. Do avoid
side effects by using the argument twice, the macros are converted into normal
functions.

This solution basically means that everything above 127 is neither a
alphabetical value nor a punctuation mark; not even printable. However, the
tests in this range are locale specific, which is not handled anyway by IRAF.

The best solution here would however be to rely on the system libc `isXXXXX()`
tests; however they may be defined as macros in `/usr/include/ctype.h`, which
makes it difficult to include in an IRAF libc function.

commit message:
revert to CFITSIO for table i/o

The libtbtables.a was changed in v2.16 to use SPP fitsio from earlier uses
of the fortran version under the assumption that they were equivalent.
However, there is a bug in the fortran version of ftdrow() when called
by the TDIFFER task in which the output table doesn't have its NAXIS2
value properly updated for FITS tables causing the task to exit.  The
cfitsio code acknowledges the value may not be correct and so uses an
internal data structure value for the 'nrows' rather than the keyword,
but equivalent functionality does not exist in the fortran version.  A
similar problem exists when inserting rows but this is not called from
any existing NTTOOLS tasks.

This change fixes a bug in the GEMINI.GSEEING task which is the only
task known to call TDIFFER.

requires some arithmetics when accessing them via `Memr` and `Memi`.

This arithmetics is done with the `P2I` and `P2R` (and other) macros
in `unix/hlib/iraf64.h` resp. `unix/hlib/iraf32.h`, and these macros
were missed in some places in `noao$digiphot/photcal/`.

commit message:
Fix keyword search in envinit

The searchs works for "set" or "reset" and is done *after* stepping
over possible whitespaces. The bug here was that "set" resp. "reset"
were searched in the string *before* whitespace removal, but the
result was applied to the string *after* the removal. This works for

but not for ("_" = space)

It is funny to see that this bug is there since 35 years, and nobody
discovered or fixed it...

For us this is important, since otherwise the "noao" variable was not
read in properly.

Fix pointer type for ZAWTBF call

correct type here to get the correct value.

author: Ole Streicher <olebole@debian.org>
commit message:
Update wait status a background process before querying it

The original code just signalled the process with signal=0 to check
whether the process still exists. However, when a process is
terminated but still no wait() was called, the process is still in the
"zombie" state, which lets the kill(pid, 0) succeed.

To overcome this, wait() needs to be called before. This is however
the only possibility to retrieve the exit status (subsequent wait()
calls to the same pid will return a failure), so the exit status needs
to be stored in prwait.c, so that it can be retrieved later with
prwait().

author: Sergio Oller <sergioller@gmail.com>
commit message:
This commit updates the parmap calls to use the new parmap arguments.

The last parmap version allows for keyword arguments to be passed to
parallelized functions like this:

    parmap.map(yourfunc, your_list, your_arg=your_val)

In order to prevent confusion between parmap arguments and keyword
arguments passed to yourfunc, it was necessary to use a common prefix
for all parmap parameters.

    parmap.map(yourfunc, your_list, your_arg=your_val, pm_parallel=True)

With this new syntax, it is easy for anyone to see that keyword arguments
starting with `pm_` are for parmap, while other arguments (here your_arg)
will be passed to the parallelized function.

That's why I had to change `parallel` to `pm_parallel`.

On the other hand, the best way to use parmap with a specific number
of CPUs is through the `pm_processes` argument, instead of creating
a multiprocessing pool manually. This has been changed in this commit
as well.

Currently the old parmap arguments are still valid, and they give
deprecation warnings so users can update the syntax. However it is best
to transition to the new arguments, as a future parmap 2.0 version
might break this backwards compatibility.

The parmap dependency in setup.py has been updated accordingly as well.

commit message:
Remove ion_mass and isotope_mass

The functionality of ion_mass and isotope_mass are subsets of the
functionality of particle_mass, and it doesn't make much sense to have
three separate functions that are designed to do the same thing.  This
commit removes these two functions so that we are left with only the
most general one: particle_mass.

"There should be one-- and preferably only one --obvious way to do
it."

One thing to be aware of is that ion_mass and isotope_mass checked to
make sure that particles were ions or isotopes, whereas particle_mass
does not.  It is better to use @particle_input to test whether or not
a particle meets the requisite criteria for a function.

commit message:
Create pytest helper classes to hold test inputs

This commit creates three classes to be used to store the callable and
arguments, and then call it.  These classes include all of the
processing to handle and validate positional and keyword arguments,
and include additional checks like making sure that functions are
indeed functions.  The goal is to hide all of this low-level stuff
from the higher-level test runner functionality during the refactoring
of run_test.

The three variations of the result test pattern are: (1) calling a
function with args & kwargs, (2) calling a class instance method, and
(3) accessing a class instance attribute to make sure that the result
matches the correct value.  The classes corresponding to this include
FunctionTestInputs, ClassMethodTestInputs, and
ClassAttributeTestInputs.

The lines that say `__tracebackhide__ = True` are instructions for
pytest to consider this a test runner function and not include
traceback information when doing the error report.

An alternative to the `call` method on these classes is to use
functools.partial, which binds arguments to a callable and creates a
new function-like thing.  I think the code is more understandable to
spell out how the function, method, or attribute is being called prior
to a test.

Warn if ion_mass assumes a particle is singly ionized

Prior to this, ion_mass silently assumed that a particle is singly
ionized if no charge information is given.  With this change, ion_mass
now warns that this assumption is being made.  I modified examples as
well.

I refactored _is_proton to use isotope_symbol and charge_state, which
cannot be done for several other _is_* functions since isotope_symbol
or charge_state calls them.  Prior to this, there were some bugs that
arose where _is_proton would return False when it should have returned
True.  These bugs got fixed in the refactoring.

* Rename variables and arguments in formulary

In preparation for renaming `plasmapy.atomic` to `plasmapy.particles`,
I went through and changed variables named `particles` to `species` to
avoid the namespace conflicts that arose when I first trying the Great
Renaming.  While I was at it, I also changed `ion_particle` to `ion`
whenever it showed up.  This changes the API, in preparation for more
changes to the API.

* Rename plasmapy.atomic to plasmapy.particles

PyCharm made this so easy!  The only thing I had to change manually
was a docstring example that imported plasmapy.atomic.  Now to check
the docstrings...  I'll be thanking Software Carpentry for teaching me
how to use grep.

* Change plasmapy.atomic to plasmapy.particles in docstrings

* Rename plasmapy.atomic to plasmapy.particles in docs

The only places where "plasmapy.atomic" should show up in the
repository are in the change log and release notes.  Those references
should stay as they are because they refer to past releases.

commit message:
Replace instances of Riot with Matrix/Element

To quote from the relevant issue:

The interesting thing here:

* Matrix is the chat platform we were and still are using;
* Riot is the old name of the particular chat client we're using;
* Element is the new name for that chat client.

> nowadays there are lots of other Matrix clients, vendors and hosting providers that demonstrate perfectly the diversity of the Matrix ecosystem.

(from the linked page)

So I'm going to standardize this to Matrix in most cases, but link to Element. I guess we could link to https://matrix.to/#/#plasmapy:openastronomy.org (I found the site by looking at what provides the ![Matrix](https://matrix.to/img/matrix-badge.svg) badge), but since Matrix is a bit niche as is, having the chat another step away and making people decide which chat client to use seems counterproductive.

author: Nick Murphy <namurphy@cfa.harvard.edu>
commit message:
Improve plasma dispersion function tests

 - I changed the argument of the plasma dispersion function from ζ
   (zeta) to w, which is another commonly used variable for the
   argument.  The screen output now only has ASCII unicode characters
   (instead of non-ASCII unicode characters).

 - I kept the use of π for pi, and now define Γ as the gamma function
   from SciPy.  The default encoding of Python 3 is UTF-8 so I do not
   expect this to cause any problems for people using PlasmaPy, but
   this usage is experimental.  This usage has the potential benefit
   of producing code that much more closely matches mathematical
   expressions, which will in turn make them more readable.  Their
   usage right now is isolated to a test rather than the main program,
   so this should give us an idea of whether or not it will cause any
   problems.

 - I added some comments that specify where the tabulated results and
   exact analytical relationships used in the tests come from.  These
   comments are separate from the docstrings and error messages.

 - I clarified and improved the formatting of some of the error
   messages.

commit message:
Generalize ion sound speed (#700)

* Generalize ion_sound_speed function

Addresses issue #316. Generalizes ion_sound_speed to work for any
case, not just for the limit when (k * lambda_D) ** 2 is small.
Additional term from Chapter 5.1, Froula, Glenzer, Luhmann and
Sheffield "Plasma Scattering of Electromagnetic Radiation".

Docstring updated to remove note about non-dispersive limit. Updated
docstring examples, and included new example with a large value for
(k * lambda_D) ** 2.

Updated tests for ion_sound_speed, and added additional tests for
the (general) large limit. Updated the assert_can_handle_nparray
pytest helper method to work for the additional parameter, "k",
added to the ion_sound_speed function.

* Update contributors list

* Fix ion_sound_speed docstring examples

* Remove duplicate parameters in examples

* Add changelog entry (#700)

* Change k and n_e to optional parameters

Specify default values for k and n_e such that if values are
not specified by the user, assume the non-dispersive limit for
ion_sound_speed.

* Fix default values for k and n_e

Change default values of k and n_e to None, and add checks to ensure
the user has given both values. Assume non-dispersive limit if user
has only given one of k or n_e. Add tests to check that a UserWarning
is thrown if only one of k or n_e has been given.

* Revert some tests back to default values (k, n_e)

* Change UserWarning to PhysicsWarning

Fix warning when only given one of (k, n_e). Change Userwarning
to PhysicsWarning.

* Restructure PhysicsWarning (for k and n_e)

commit message:
Create _check_quantity plus tests

This method checks that an object is a Quantity with acceptable units
and valid numerical values.  Optional keyword arguments provide some
flexibility, including options to allow or disallow Quantities with
negative values (e.g., for densities), complex numbers, or infinities.
This method is intended to simplify code for calculating things like
plasma parameters, since this would otherwise require significant
duplication of code.

An alternative is the quantity_input decorator in astropy.  However,
quantity_input does not check for NaNs or other constraints on values.
Moreover, there are some functions in parameters.py that allow units
of two different types (e.g., finding a gyroradius can be done using
either a perpendicular velocity, or a temperature if you want to use a
thermal velocity).

In the future we might want to turn this into a decorator, or to
propose upstream changes to quantity_input.

Improve error messages in atomic tests

around argument, whereas f"{argument}" will not.  Using repr makes it
easier to have an error message print out the exact expression that is
causing the error which makes debugging easier.

commit message:
Add inplace kwarg to ionize & recombine in Particle

Prior to this commit, I had Particle.ionize and Particle.recombine
both change the instance of Particle that these methods were called
from to the ionized/recombined Particle, and return the new
ionized/recombined Particle as well.  This commit adds the `inplace`
keyword argument that allows users to specify that the Particle should
or should not be changed to the new Particle or returned.  The name
`inplace` is the convention used in Pandas.

Co-authored by: Dominik Stańczak <stanczakdominik@gmail.com>

commit message:
Update pycodestyle defaults

Whitespace is required around arithmetic operators to improve
readability by making it easier to parse equations.

For the time being I set E241 and E242 so that there has to be no more
than one space after a comma.  There may be times where having things
aligned will make it more readable, so we might wish to revisit this
in the future.

W504 is set so that during a line break, a line should start with the
binary operator (as opposed to the previous line ending with it).

   handle antineutrons and antiprotons (which each have a baryon

commit message:
Update Particle class and @particle_input + tests

These are significant updates to pass tests.

In @particle_input, I added narrative comments.  I also fixed a bug
where an argument that was already a Particle was not checked to make
sure that it fit the required criteria.  I tried to make the error
messages as clear as I could.

In Particle, I fixed a bunch of bugs in order for tests to pass,
especially related to determination of masses, categories, and
exceptions.  I updated some docstrings too.

I changed Particle.__eq__ to compare only the particle symbol to
address some weird problems where two electron Particle objects were
not being determined to be equal.  I suspect that this may have been
because I used a lambda function in the defaultdict declaration which
didn't register as the same in both instances, but I did not figure
this out for certain.  We may wish to do this more carefully in the
future to make sure more of the attributes are equal.

commit message:
Remove n_e kwarg and change default values

Prior to this commit, it was possible to provide number density
information to IonizationState through the n_e, n_elem, and
ionic_fractions arguments.  Having both n_e and n_elem is pretty
redundant.  Because n_elem is much more natural of a way to do this, I
removed n_e as an argument.  It may be worth having a @n_e.setter
function just in case there are times where that would be more
convenient.

I also set the default values of n_elem and T_e to np.nan times
units. Also x.n_elem and x.T_e will return np.nan times units if these
values are not set.  This seems more appropriate than using None as
the default.  I need vegan ice cream.

commit message:
Create class for expected test outcomes in pytest-helpers

The ExpectedTestOutcome class created here is an attempt to put all
responsibilities for storing and processing information about a test
outcome into one place.  This functionality has heretofore been in
our test runner function, run_test.  Because run_test contains a
whole bunch of functionality in one place, it will be much cleaner
to separate responsibilities into different classes.

I expect that this class will be used rarely outside of PlasmaPy,
so I tried to write it so that the attributes are more readable. I
don't know if this class actually should have an expected_outcome
attribute, because that is in there for the time being for human
convenience.

I will have to go back and finish up the comparison operators like
__eq__, but that will require first finishing the class that
represents that actual test outcome.  Also, we should account for
the case where the expected outcome is a unit (i.e., that the
result has units of barn-megaparsecs, for example).

commit message:
Remove message kwarg in pytest.raises and pytest.warns

In pytest.raises, the message argument has been used to provide a test
failure message, but it has gotten confused with the match argument
which is used to check the message from the exception to be tested so
it is being deprecated.  I changed the usage to:

    with pytest.fails(SomeException):
        should_raise_exception()
	pytest.fails("should_raise_exception() did not raise anything")

Also, we had pytest.warns(..., message="...") at one point, though it
appears pytest.warns does not do anything with the message kwarg to
begin with.  That had to be changed into a grumpier try except block.

The interesting thing here:

* Matrix is the chat platform we were and still are using;

* Element is the new name for that chat client.

> nowadays there are lots of other Matrix clients, vendors and hosting providers that demonstrate perfectly the diversity of the Matrix ecosystem.

commit message:
Refactor dependency checks in __init__.py

Prior to this, there were separate checks for NumPy and Astropy to
make sure that they were at least the minimum version.  This commit
consolidates those two checks into _check_versions where the argument
of that function is a dictionary with package names as keys and
minimum version strings as the corresponding items.  There's also a
separate _check_python with a separate __minimum_python_version__
variable which makes things easier than including that
__check_versions.

By reducing the number of lines in this file, I'm pretty sure this
will make coveralls grumpy because the coverage percentage will go
down...

commit message:
Significant updates to parameters.py and tests

Adding lots of tests, including numerical tests for most functions.
Expanding docstrings, in particular to document what exceptions are
raised.  Changed "from astropy import units as u" to "from astropy
import units" since having units.whatever will be more readable to
someone newly reading the code.  Changed some positional arguments of
functions to keywords, and required inputs to ion_sound_speed to be
keywords (since it might be easy to mix up the electron and ion
temperatures if they could be inputted as positional arguments).
Continued put _check_quantity and _check_relativistic to check inputs
and outputs of functions, and hoping that nobody notices until later
that these should be changed into decorators.

commit message:
Refactor test_atomic.py with run_test

This is a major refactoring of tests of atomic functions using the
test helper function, run_test.

Previously there were several separate test functions and tables for
each function.  Moreover, for each atomic function there were several
separate test functions and tables to test the results, warnings, and
exceptions.

In this change, there is one table for each atomic function that
includes the positional arguments, optionally the keyword arguments,
and the expected outcome (which may be a warning or exception as well
as the expected result).  These are all run by the same new test
function which calls run_test.

I also added some code to prepend the function in each set of inputs
in the each test table, in order to avoid having to repeat the same
function over and over in each table.

There is also some code to add in inputs for a bunch of different
functions for different exceptions but for the same set of inputs.

It would be helpful to also have a function that tests to make sure
that two calls with equivalent inputs will yield equivalent outputs.
This would be helpful for inputs like 'p+' and 'H-1+' in atomic.

There are still some tests that I need to refactor into the run_test
formulation, and I may see if there are some simpler ways to go about
this.  I am still wondering if an object-oriented approach would end
up being cleaner in the long run.

commit message:
Update test documentation (#542)

This pull request updates the testing guide in our development
guide since it needed to be updated to reflect that we are using
Codecov now intead of Coveralls, as well as a bunch of other
things.

I prepended a motivation section since the plasma physics
community doesn't always recognize the importance of testing.
I split the other sections up into how to run tests, write tests,
and use code coverage reports.

I added a discussion about using `python setup.py test`.  I'm
wondering if it would be helpful to add some more information
later on about the integration with setuptools, though maybe that
would be best described in the code itself.  

I expanded the discussion about testing warnings and exceptions,
and tried to change function names in examples to say more
explicitly what the function does (even though the function names
are now kind of boring).

I provided a more thorough discussion of the pytest helpers that
I contributed a while back.  I still think of this feature as
experimental, though I personally really like it since it makes
it much easier to write tests that compare Quantity objects to
within a tolerance and to check warnings and exceptions.

I kept the discussion on fixtures brief as suggested, though we
might want to put an example of the usage we might expect for
plasma physics in the documentation later on.

I updated the discussion on using coverage reports with Codecov,
and described how to generate these reports locally.

I added mypy cache directories to .gitignore in case we ever end
up using mypy, and updated our contributing guide.

commit message:
Expand class that compares actual & expected test results

The single responsibility of the CompareActualExpected class is to
generate descriptive error messages, as necessary, for the different
reasons why tests fail.  This class accounts for cases that expect an
exception to be raised, a warning to be issued, and/or a value to be
returned.

Whereas run_test had a bunch of these things piled together in one
function, I broke up the different error message creators so that each
one has its own method in the class.  The last method in the class
(_make_errmsg_if_necessary) contains the logic of which method goes
with which conditions.  I decided against a nested structure for these
conditionals because doing otherwise started to make my brain hurt.

I still need to polish the error messages and make sure that the
correct error message matches the correct pattern.

When writing tests that fall under the result test pattern, I found
myself writing essentially the same error messages over and over for
different tests.  The goal is to isolate all of that boilerplate stuff
in this class so that we need not rewrite the same pattern over and
over.  Moreover, this allows more detailed checks to be performed.
The goal of this effort is to greatly simplify our existing test suite
as well as the process of writing new tests for situations that fall
under the result test pattern.  Once this class is completed, I should
have all of the functionality needed to rewrite run_test into
something much shorter (my goal is less than ten lines!).

Exception docstrings and too negative charge states

actually correspond to the exceptions that are called in the code.

Making some of these functions raise a UserWarning when the charge
state is -4 or below.  When I asked my upstairs neighbor (a chemist)
what the most negative charge that she has ever run across, she said
-2 and that even that required special conditions.  We could thus
possibly change this to -3 or below, but there could be some instances
where a -3 charge state could be what a user wants.

commit message:
Creating _check_relativistic and tests

Creating a method that will check whether or not a Quantity
representing a velocity is relativstic.  This method is primarily for
use in checking plasma parameter calculations to see if we end up with
Alfven speeds exceeding 0.1*c, and raising UserWarnings if it does.
The Lorentz factor for 0.1*c is about 1.005.

A possibility for refactoring in the future would be to create a
decorator that will check whether or not the velocity returned by a
function is relativistic.  This would probably be more Pythonic, but
on the other hand, I'm getting kind of sleepy.

Also: renaming quantities.py to checks.py.

commit message:
Remove fetch-depth for actions/checkout

When checking out a GitHub repository in a workflow, we had been setting
fetch-depth=0 because we intended to only include the most recent commit.
However, fetch-depth=0 causes the entire history to be downloaded. Oops.
We should have had fetch-depth=1 since that downloads only the most
recent commit, but since that's the default, we do not need to set
fetch-depth at all.

commit message:
Use isinstance on (int, np.integer) instead of int

I noticed that using isinstance(n, int) was returning False when n was
a numpy.int64 object, for example.  On the World Wide Web™ I found we
could instead do isinstance(n, (int, numpy.integer)).  I made this
change in a bunch of atomic modules for Z and mass_numb.

I did not yet change the docstrings or type hints to reflect that
numpy.integer types are allowed, and am debating whether or not it
would be best to do so.  The docstrings and type hints will be more
explicit with allowed types if we say that numpy.integer types are
allowed, but the docstrings and especially the type hints will get
more difficult to read.  It would be helpful if we could make this
notation more compact.  If we end up checking type hints with mypy, we
might need to at least update the type hints.

commit message:
Add ionize and recombine methods to Particle class

These methods take a Particle object and run __init__ again for the
same element/isotope but for a different charge.  The ionize method
will raise an InvalidIonError if a bare nucleus is attempted to be
ionized.  The recombine method will issue a warning if the charge
becomes negative; however, no exception will be raised in that case.

One behavior that I'm not certain about is both running __init__ again
and returning the new Particle instance.  We may wish to have just one
behavior or the other.  If we have just the in-place
re-initialization, then we would not be able to do comparisons like
Particle("Fe 5+").recombine() == Particle("Fe 4+") which require the
new Particle instance to be returned.

commit message:
Have mass_energy use mass of nucleon instead

The mass_energy function and Particle.mass_energy had just been
calculating the mass energy for isotopes based on the total mass, with
nuclear_mass_energy and Particle.nuclear_mass_energy being what
calculated the mass energy of the nucleus of an isotope.

The mass_energy function will generally be used for nuclear reactions,
where the nuclear mass energy is the only important quantity.  This
commit removes nuclear_mass_energy and Particle.nuclear_mass_energy
and makes mass_energy and Particle.mass_energy calculate the mass
energy based off of the mass of the nucleus of an isotope or nucleon.

commit message:
Update main __init__.py

(1) I added a comment that dunder notation should be reserved for the
special objects that have been defined by the Python team, and that
PlasmaPy-specific variables should just have an underscore.  I learned
this recently from the following blog post:

"Python double-under, double-wonder" by Andrew Montalenti
http://www.pixelmonkey.org/2013/04/11/python-double-under-double-wonder

Here's a direct quote:

"Never, ever, invent your own dunders — Python leaves you with a
number of clean namespaces (classes, modules, etc.) for your own
code. Use them! The core Python team reserved a somewhat ugly
namespace for themselves — don’t trample all over their compromise by
stealing their names."

(2) I added ModuleNotFoundError as another exception to be caught
along with ImportError.  I don't think that any of the commands in
that section of imports will raise this; however, we might add
different import syntaxes in the future so we should catch these
exceptions just in case.

commit message:
Update Particle class

I implemented ParticleZoo in the place where categories (such as
'lepton', 'fermion', etc.) are assigned.  Previously, I used exec to
execute the strings of the commands that I created.  However, this
does not play well with PyCharm and other static type checkers that
have a harder time interpreting what is happenening in lines that use
exec.

Previously, the private variables in the Particle class were
initialized by using eval on strings such as "self._mass = None".
This also does not play well with PyCharm, etc.  I changed the way
private variables are initialized so that there are instead a bunch of
statements instead of a loop with eval.

I changed a few flags related to coverage reports to better reflect
what I think does not need to be tested as opposed to what we should
know is not being tested.

commit message:
Create classes to represent ionization state distributions (#404)

This pull request creates the IonizationState class to represent the
ionization state of a single element or isotope, and the
IonizationStates class to represent the ionization states of multiple
elements or isotopes.  

These classes were written in conjunction with another project to do
non-equilibrium ionization (NEI) modeling:

   https://github.com/NEI-modeling/NEI

There is still room for refactoring and improvements, but it looks
like it's in a good enough state to merge and avoid becoming another
"transport PR incident".  For the full commit history, see #404 on
GitHub.  The commit history is summarized here.

 - I included a lot of flexibility in the inputs; in particular, I
   allowed the ionic fractions to be set as either array-like or a
   Quantity with units of number density.  I allowed the base
   particles to be either elements or isotopes (though not both the
   element and isotopes from that element because that could involve
   double counting).

 - For type hint annotations, I because using numbers.Integral and
   numbers.Real since they are the abstract classes that different
   integers and floats inherit from.  I did imports like `from numbers
   import Real` because having the full `numbers.Real` and
   `typing.Dict` in the function definition reduced readability.

 - Early on, I used an n_H attribute in IonizationStates to represent
   the number density of hydrogen.  That would make sense in
   astrophysical plasmas, but would not make sense for many laboratory
   plasmas.  I changed that to be a number density scaling factor.

 - I chose to have undefined attributes default to numpy.nan (possibly
   times an attribute) instead of raising an exception.  This way,
   operations can continue to be performed even if there are some nan
   values.  This is in line with how numpy operations work.  I am
   wondering, though, if it would be worth including a warning when
   there are nans.

 - Using nans caused headaches because numpy.nan == numpy.nan
   evaluates to False, so the equality measures (in particular, in
   __eq__) ended up being kind of complicated.  It may be good to have
   a helper function called something like `same_enough` that does
   this sort of equality comparison and accounts for Quantity
   comparisons as well as comparisons to within a tolerance.

 - I created an info method for IonizationState(s) to print out
   quicklook information.  This was originally in __repr__, but pytest
   error messages ended up being very messy with all the breakline
   characters, so we decided to move it to its own method.

 - For an IonizationState instance, __getitem__ will return a State
   corresponding to a particular ionization level.  I did not include
   __setitem__ for IonizationState because we need to change ionic
   fractions as a whole because of the normalization constraint.
   Iterating through an instance involves iterating through each State
   instance.  I chose not to allow slicing for an IonizationState
   instance because having a State instance with more than one level
   would be pretty much like having something really close to an
   IonizationState instance.

 - For an IonizationStates instance, __getitem__ will return an
   IonizationState instance corresponding to a particular element or
   isotope.  I included __setitem__ to allow new ionic fractions to be
   set.  Item assignment will also often work for number densities, so
   long as there isn't potential for contradiction with, e.g.,
   abundance information that is previously partially provided when
   the number density scaling factor is absent.  Iterating through an
   IonizationStates instance involves iterating through
   IonizationState instances for the different elements/isotopes.

 - I allowed both abundances and base 10 log_abundances, since it is
   common in astronomy to use both.

 - I made Particle class instances hashable so that they can be used
   as keys in dicts.  I returned the hash of the result from repr so
   that it is different than the hash for the particle symbol string.
   I wanted to make sure that the hash of a Particle instance was
   different than the hash of the particle's symbol, since
   Particle('H') == 'H' should evaluate to True and there could be
   some confusion as a result.  Usually, only immutable objects should
   be given __hash__.  Particle is not strictly immutable, but should
   be thought of as such.

Remaining work includes:
 
 - Expand the docstrings with more examples.  In particular, put
   documentation for dunder methods into the main class docstrings.
   since it doesn't show up in online docs.

 - Change the State namedtuple to a class so that it can contain
   checks that the parameters have the correct properties.

 - Expand test coverage of exceptions, and also make sure that the
   exceptions that show up are appropriate.

 - Clean up the tests for IonizationState(s).  I suspect that some of
   these tests would be highly appropriate for fixtures.

 - Develop the methods to (1) calculate collisional ionization
   equilibrium and (2) model non-equilibrium ionization plasmas.  The
   atomic date required for both are pretty much the same.  A
   difficulty is that there is going to be some density dependence on
   atomic rates as well as temperature dependence because some
   mechanisms only occur at, e.g., lower densities.  Including
   photoionization is probably way out of scope, though that is
   functionality that will be needed somewhere in the PlasmaPy/
   Astropy/SunPy software ecosystem.

 - We should develop functionality to plot a charge state
   distribution, perhaps as a method in IonizationState.  Marcus
   DuPont in the NEI repository mentioned above has written some
   plotting routines that would be really good to implement.

 - It would probably be helpful to allow negatively charged ions to be
   included.  In some instances, H- will be important, for example as
   a source of opacity in stellar atmospheres.  Doubly negatively
   charged ions will probably be exceptionally rare in plasmas.

 - In IonizationState, I chose the Z_most_abundant method to be a list
   since there will be times when more than one ionization level will
   be the most important.  If Z_most_abundant were to sometimes return
   an integer and sometimes return a list, it would make dealing with
   it more of a pain for users.  I'm not sure if it would be better to
   turn it into a tuple.

Some additional thoughts:

 - We could use __add__ to allow adding of IonizationState(s)
   instances to form an IonizationStates instance.  This seems lower
   priority to me since I don't think I would use it very often.

 - Another possibility would be to consolidate IonizationState and
   IonizationStates.  It can be confusing to have similar names.  A
   caveat with consolidating them is that IonizationStates.__getitem__
   yields an IonizationState instance.  

 - One possible bug is that item assignment to one of the dictionary
   attributes can cause problems.  If we do something like
   `ionstates.ionic_fractions['H'] = some_value` then `some_value`
   could be assigned without going through all of the checks.  We
   could possibly create a class for such attributes, but for the time
   being it's probably best to just do `ionstates['H'] = some_value`.

 - We probably want to look more into how the State namedtuple and
   IonizationState(s) classes relate to different classes in the
   fiasco pacakge that represent ions or elements.  There is
   definitely more room for collaboration.

 - I started using pytest.fail() for test failures besides
   AssertionErrors.  It would probably be good to use this in
   run_test, with it specified to ignore the traceback within
   run_test.

It has been really helpful to talk about this PR with Chengcai Shen,
Will Barnes, Marcus DuPont, and Dominik Stańczak.  Many thanks! 😸

commit message:
Put ion_mass's singly charged assumption back in

Up until now, ion_mass has worked for a bunch of particles that are
not ions.  In particular, if an element or isotope was given with no
charge information, then ion_mass assumed that the particle was singly
ionized.  I regret making the decision to default to this assumption
since "explicit is better than implicit".  It would be better to make
people write the charge information explicitly in an ion's symbol.

The calculation of ion mass by the Particle class does not make the
assumption that a particle is singly ionized, so ion_mass lost this
capability when I switched over to using @particle_input.  I just put
this functionality back in, along with a few solar masses worth of
DeprecationWarnings.

Some of the other test failures were caused by small discrepancies
from when a Constant is used versus a Quantity with the same value.

I also wrote a particle_mass function that is much more general, and
can be used for functions such as thermal_speed that do not require
charged particles.  This still needs docstrings and tests.

commit message:
Use ~ to return antiparticle of special particles

I used the __invert__ dunder method in the Particle class to allow the
unary operator to return the antiparticle of the particle associated
with a Particle instance.  This only works for special particles and
antiparticles, and thus will not work for any atoms or ions except for
protons.  Magic methods are awesome!

commit message:
Remove caching in ParticleList (+ other updates)

Suppose one element of ParticleList is a CustomParticle. Then suppose
someone modifies the mass of that CustomParticle directly, without
modifying the identities of the particles within the list. Then the
cached values of mass would no longer be valid. This will probably not
be a common issue, but it could cause unexpected and difficult to track
down problems. It'll be safer and cleaner to avoid caching. We can
revisit caching if/when there's a situation where it ends up being needed.

commit message:
Extend tests for plasma_dispersion_func

I added a test against a power series expansion that I think is valid
around 0 + 0j, and added tests for the first five zeros of the panda
dispersion function.

I increased the accuracy of many of these tests by using mpmath to do
this at greater precision:

    from mpmath import j, sqrt, exp, erf, findroot
    def Z(w):
        return j * sqrt(pi) * exp(-w**2) * (1 + erf(j * w))

To find the roots at greater precision than in the appendix of Plasma
Waves by Swanson (2nd edition), I did:

    findroot(Z, 4.106_107_271 - 3.725_948_279j)

commit message:
Add first draft of a class to store outcomes of tests

I created the ActualTestOutcome class in order to call the
function/method or access a class attribute and record the outcome of
that call.  The outcome could be an exception, a warning, a returned
value, and/or both a warning and a value.  The idea is to consolidate
all of the exception handling and context environments into one place
so that it can be isolated from the high level calls.  This commit
lays out the overall structure of ActualTestOutcome, and is a good
place to look to get a big picture view before a whole bunch more
attributes and processing functionality gets added.  I wanted to make
sure to commit this now, as writing this class made my brain hurt.

author: Nick Murphy <namurphy@cfa.harvard.edu>
commit message:
Increase pycodestyle maximum line length to 89

The topic of the maximum line length came up in a recent code review
session.  The PEP 8 limit is 79 characters because (1) really long
lines adversely impact readability, (2) wrapping of long lines by
editors disrupts the flow, and (3) this line length makes it easier to
display two windows of code side by side.  The 79 character limit
resulted in some awkward line breaks using backslashes in the Particle
class, whereas the code would be more readable were it just be on the
same line.  Those of us who were present came to a consensus that we
should increase the line length so that we can avoid awkward line
breaks.

This commit increases the maximum line length by ten characters so
that we can avoid these awkward line breaks while still avoiding
really long lines.  Comments and docstrings should continue to be
wrapped at 72 characters to make things more readable, and the 79
character limit is still suggested.
